intake: believer - practicing Roman Catholic (weekly Mass, confession, Thomist-leaning on the philosophy side), chemistry grad student who reads arguments the way I read a mechanism: looking for the step that was skipped.

walk.note: Fair description of how I actually started; an inherited story did answer the need.
The hidden premise that testimony is not evidence is wrong, but natural theology is where I already stand, so the move carries me anyway.
Classical theism does not deny a personal God; Aquinas's God of pure being has intellect and will, so 'a God who chooses is a subject classical theism denies' is simply false.
The premise that divine action must be statistically legible in a prayer protocol is a vending-machine model of God that no serious theology ever promised.
I agree mind does not reduce to matter, though I would say it as Aquinas's hylomorphism rather than Descartes's two substances.
I grant all the chemistry; dependence of mind on brain does not entail identity with brain, and the move slides from one to the other.
Granting materialism, this is just correcting the vocabulary; fields and energy are not 'matter' in the old sense.
That physics gives structure but not what bears it is a real gap, but a gap in physicalism does not deliver the conclusion that reality is at bottom mind.
Granting the dream, a dream wants a dreamer; Lichtenberg's worry is noted but does not move me.
Strawson's point is sound and matches how I already see other people.
I would choose mercy too; for me it is also commanded, but as a choice it is the one I make.
Docta ignorantia is home ground for a Catholic; the entropy sentence is odd but does not break the step.
Hope is a choice I make, though the author's Religion2 rests on Mercy-as-system where mine rests on a person.
A maker worth hoping toward would know simply and forget nothing; the move's last sentence undercuts itself, but the destination is right.
There is no stated reason at all; 'more of a bargain than an argument' tells me the premise is missing but not what the bargain was.

'To think is to ignore' is true of attention-limited minds like mine and is then quietly generalized to every possible mind; the move itself admits Aquinas's non-discursive knowing was never shown incoherent.
Granting no maker, suffering is still bad for the one who suffers; the critics' grounding question is mine, but the step itself holds.
I agree subjective goods are not fungible, and the move honestly admits the need to be remembered is a motive, not evidence.
I would not park hope on data about a system that does not exist; from Dualism2 I would go back to Religion2, not wait at a question mark.

first_exit.why: The dilemma turns on the claim that classical theism denies a God who chooses, but that is not what Aquinas or any classical theist holds; God as being itself has intellect and will and acts freely. The missing premise is a definition of 'classical theism' that nobody in the tradition would sign, so the hiddenness argument never gets started.

comment: Your route against God rests on two misdescriptions of the position it is leaving: at move 3 that classical theism denies a God who chooses, and at move 16 that every possible mind must think by ignoring; fix either and the first turn's atheism and the second turn's atheism both lose their load-bearing premise. What struck me most is that Dualism2 hopes to be remembered as a self by a conscious other, and move 14 already told you what such a rememberer would have to be: one who knows without reasoning and forgets nothing. You have drawn the shape of the God you set aside and left the name off it.
